opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's a tendency to see "narrow" as a limitation, but for AlphaFold it was really the point. We picked a problem that was extraordinarily well defined: you give me an amino acid sequence, I give you the three-dimensional coordinates of the atoms. There was a clear notion of what a right answer looked like, decades of experimental structures in the Protein Data Bank to learn from, and a community benchmark in CASP that told you, blind, whether you were actually any good. That combination is rare, and it's what let us make real progress rather than just plausible-looking progress.

When the scope is tight, you can be relentlessly honest with yourself. You can measure, you can see exactly where the model fails, and you can put serious domain knowledge into the architecture: things about geometry, about how residues relate to each other, about evolutionary information in multiple sequence alignments. A lot of what made AlphaFold work wasn't some general trick; it was many specific ideas that only make sense because we understood the problem deeply.

The other part is that narrow doesn't mean small in impact. Structure prediction sits underneath a huge amount of biology. Making one well-defined thing work reliably turned out to be enormously useful to people doing very different science: drug discovery, enzyme design, understanding disease mutations. Researchers could take a tool they trusted and plug it into their own questions. I'd rather build something that does one important thing extremely well and that experimentalists believe, than something broad that's impressive in a demo but that nobody can rely on at the bench.

So for me the lesson is: find a problem where you can tell whether you're right, where it matters if you're right, and then go very deep. Generality can come later, but trust comes from accuracy, and accuracy usually comes from focus.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the narrowness was the point, not a limitation we tolerated. When we set out, the question wasn't "how do we build a general model of biology," it was "can we predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein from its sequence." That's a problem with a very crisp definition, decades of carefully curated experimental data in the PDB, and a benchmark in CASP where you genuinely can't fool yourself. You either get the structure right or you don't, and the answer comes back from people who have no interest in flattering you.

That specificity let us do things you simply can't do with a vague target. We could bake real physical and biological knowledge directly into the architecture. The fact that proteins live in three-dimensional space, that pairs of residues co-evolve, that atoms can't overlap, that a chain has to be geometrically consistent. Every one of those inductive biases was a bet that we could test, and when a bet failed we knew quickly. If you're trying to be general about everything, you lose that feedback loop. You're never sure whether a change helped because it was correct or because it moved the loss on some average that doesn't mean anything.

The other thing is that a narrow problem can still be a profound one. Protein structure sits at the center of so much biology that solving it well, rather than solving many things poorly, turned out to be enormously useful. People sometimes assume that scope and impact scale together, and I don't think that's right. Depth on the right problem buys you more than breadth on an ill-defined one.

And honestly, it kept us intellectually honest about what we had and hadn't done. AlphaFold predicts structures. It doesn't tell you how a protein moves, it doesn't tell you what it binds without further work, it doesn't understand a cell. Being clear about those boundaries is what let the scientific community trust the thing where it does work, and that trust is a large part of why it got used at all.

astra-6.text:
I think the narrow scope gives you a very clear way to make progress. We’re asking a specific question: given a protein’s sequence, can we predict its structure? That’s an extraordinarily difficult question, but we can measure how well we’re answering it. We can compare a prediction with an experimentally determined structure and find out whether an idea actually helped.

And narrow doesn’t mean unimportant. Protein structure connects to a huge range of biological questions. You can focus intensely on one problem, solve it well enough to be useful, and then enable people with very different expertise to do things you hadn’t anticipated.

It also helps clarify the limits. Predicting a structure isn’t the same as explaining everything that protein does, or solving biology. But it can give you a powerful piece of the puzzle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think having a narrow scope gives you a very clear connection between what you build and whether it actually works. With AlphaFold, we’re asking a specific question: given this protein sequence, can we predict its structure? It’s an enormously difficult question, but you can measure progress against experiments.

That clarity lets you make strong choices about the model, the data, and how you evaluate it. You don’t need to solve every aspect of intelligence to produce something scientifically useful. And narrow doesn’t necessarily mean small in impact: protein structure is a specific problem that matters to a huge range of biological questions.
